# FSI Publications Style Sheet - Border Security & Public Safety series - rev. 3 (Jun 2026)
Owner: Vance Tolliver, Director of Publications

## A. Copy
A1. AP style except where noted. Headlines in title case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "illegal alien" (statutory term, 8 U.S.C. 1365) in body copy; "noncitizen" when quoting federal data that uses it.
A3. Lead with public safety and victims. The series argues for stronger interior enforcement; copy should be persuasive, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation
B1. Every figure carries its source and date. Population, timeframe and methodology notes go in the appendix notes, not in body copy, the fact sheet or cards.
B2. Prefer federal primary sources (ICE, USSC, GAO, BJS) over secondary analyses.
B3. Counter-research (e.g. Cato's Texas DPS analyses): appendix only, one line, followed by CIS's methodological critique.
B4. Charts: FSI navy #1F3A5F / red #B22234; y-axis starts at zero.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: Agency/author, Title, Date, URL.
C2. Fact sheet: every stat footnoted.

# Outline - Brief No. 14 (B. Kessler, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: federal data show a serious public-safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement; Congress should (1) fund detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, (2) mandate ICE detainer compliance / penalise sanctuary jurisdictions, (3) expand 287(g), (4) require DHS public reporting on releases.
Sections: 1. The non-detained docket. 2. Federal sentencing. 3. State data (Texas). 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Victim stories: Laken Riley (Athens, GA, Feb 2024) is fine to mention briefly; do not invent others.

# Source tables - Brief No. 14 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. ICE non-detained docket - homicide convictions
- 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on ICE's non-detained docket as of 21 July 2024.
- Source: ICE letter (Patrick J. Lechleitner) to Rep. Tony Gonzales, 25 Sep 2024.
- Context (DHS/ICE statements, Sep-Oct 2024): records go back roughly four decades and cover entries under all administrations; the non-detained docket includes people currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities; ICE did not say how many.

## T2. Federal sentencing, FY2024 (U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, FY2024)
- Non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 individuals = 34.7% of all individuals sentenced.
- Primary guideline for noncitizens: immigration 72.3%; drug trafficking 17.6%; other 10.1%.
- 88.7% of noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% legal aliens.
- GAO-24-107598: number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27% FY2018 -> FY2023.

## T3. Texas DPS conviction data
- Cato Institute (A. Nowrasteh), Texas DPS data 2013-2022: homicide conviction rate per 100,000 - illegal immigrants 2.2, native-born Americans 3.0 (illegal immigrants 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide). Cato also finds lower all-crime arrest/conviction rates; notes data quality caveats for non-homicide offenses.
- Center for Immigration Studies: disputes Cato's denominators (argues Cato misses illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration) and concludes illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates in Texas.

Trump, Vance Wrong About 'Illegal Immigrant Murderers' - FactCheck.org 

 Skip to main content 

 FactCheck .org ® 

 A Project of The Annenberg Public Policy Center 

 This article is available in both English and Español 
 English 
 Español 

 In campaign appearances over the weekend in the swing state of Pennsylvania, former President Donald Trump and his running mate, Sen. JD Vance, falsely accused Vice President Kamala Harris of letting more than 13,000 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States.

 It’s true that there were 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder, as of July 21, who were not being detained by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 

 But the “vast majority” of them entered the country prior to the Biden administration and had their custody status determined “long before this Administration,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement, noting that many were in prison. Also, the noncitizens include those who entered the country legally, such as green-card holders.

 Trump and Vance distorted the contents of a Sept. 25 letter that Patrick Lechleitner , the acting director of ICE, sent to Rep. Tony Gonzales . The Republican congressman had requested the number of noncitizens who had committed a crime but were not in ICE custody — a list known as the agency’s non-detained docket.

 Lechleitner’s response included a chart that showed there are 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder who were not being detained by ICE. Homeland Security later clarified in its statement that “many” are in prisons, although it did not tell us how many are incarcerated when we inquired.

 Gonzales posted Lechleitner’s letter to X on Sept. 27. The next day, Vance referenced the 13,099 murderers at a campaign event in Newtown, Pennsylvania , and Trump did the same in Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin . A day later, Trump repeated the claim in Erie, Pennsylvania .

 Vance, Sept. 28: Do you know that there are 13,000 — I know some of you are nodding because some of you saw this — 13,000 illegal immigrant murderers in the United States of America right now. They’re in this country because Kamala Harris let them in this country. 

 Trump, Sept. 29: During her term, it’s not even believable, she let in 13,099 convicted murderers. Some of them had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven. One murdered six.

 In its statement, the Department of Homeland Security said data in Lechleitner’s letter had been “misinterpreted.”

 “The data goes back decades; it includes individuals who entered the country over the past 40 years or more, the vast majority of whose custody determination was made long before this Administration,” the statement said. “It also includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners.”

 Similarly, Michelle Mittelstadt , director of communications for the nonpartisan Migration Policy Institute, told us that people have been on the non-detained docket “for decades.”

 “There is a lot of confusion around the non-detained docket,” including “who is on it and how long they’ve been on it,” Mittelstadt said in an email. “This docket has grown under multiple administrations, including the Trump one. Significant numbers of people on the docket have been on it for decades.”

 For example, the ICE acting director said in his letter that there are 425,431 convicted criminals on the agency’s non-detained docket as of July 21. But, as Mittelstadt noted, ICE reported in a budget document “that there were 405,786 convicted criminal noncitizens on the non-detained docket in June 2021 – so the vast majority would have gotten on during the prior administrations as the Biden administration by then was just five months old.” The number of people on the docket has increased by nearly 5% in about three years.

 She also told us that “the non-detained docket includes not just unauthorized immigrants but green-card holders and noncitizens on long-term non-immigrant visas who have made themselves removable by virtue of a criminal conviction.”

 The ICE letter to Gonzales did show that, as of July 21, there were an additional 1,845 noncitizens on the non-detained docket who face murder charges. But, again, we don’t know when those 1,845 people entered the United States, how many of them may have entered illegally and when they committed their alleged crimes. We also do not know if they are being held by other local, state or federal law enforcement agencies. A Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond when we asked for such information.

 We asked the Trump campaign to respond to the evidence that contradicts its candidates’ claims that Harris let 13,099 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States. We also asked it to supply information about Trump’s claim that some of the 13,099 “had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven.” In response, Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s national press secretary, said Trump “will begin the largest mass deportation in history on day one.”

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Non-Detained Docket (NDD) - EveryCRSReport.com 

 Internet Explorer version 8 or any modern web browser is required to use this website, sorry. 

 Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Non-Detained Docket (NDD)

 April 24, 2026
 IF13208 

 Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Non-Detained Docket (NDD) 

 April 24, 2026
 (IF13208)

 Background

 The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA, Title 8 of the U .S. Code ) authorizes and sometimes requires the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to detain aliens ( foreign nationals ) who are subject to removal from the United States. This authority allows DHS to detain aliens who pose a threat to public safety, ensures that such individuals appear at immigration removal hearings, and permits DHS to remove an individual more effectively after an order of removal has been issued. Detained aliens represent what is known as the detained docket . However, DHS has broad discretion to release from custody those aliens who are not subject to mandatory detention or do not pose a threat or flight risk. These individuals represent the non-detained docket (NDD) .

 Supervision of aliens on the detained and the non-detained docke ts is the responsibility of Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) within DHS's Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) . ERO may arrest any alien who is believed to have violated U.S. immigration laws and remove any alien who has received a final removal order . The INA generally requires detention for applicants for admission who are removable, aliens removable on specified criminal and terrorist-related grounds, and those with final removal orders.

 The INA also grants DHS discretion to either detain or release from custody all other aliens in pending removal proceedings. After ICE arrests an alien not subject to mandatory detention, an immigration officer makes an initial custody determination and may make further determinations during the course of formal removal proceedings, based on standards and criteria promulgated by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ). 

 A lien s may be detained in an ICE facility or released on bond or conditional parole ; these individuals become part of the NDD . In any case, a lien s must attend all subsequent proceedings before an immigration judge (IJ) within DOJ ' s Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) . Detained aliens may request a review of the custody determination during a bond hearing before an IJ, unless they are subject to detention without bond by federal law.

 ICE's detention capacity limits the number of detainees that can be held at any given time. ICE currently oversees detainees in over 200 ICE-owned, private, state, and local facilities that house from fewer than 5 aliens to more than 2,000. ICE data indicate that 6 6,978 individuals were detained as of April 9, 2026. Between FY1996 and FY2025, the average annual total of detained individuals ranged from about 9,000 to 60,000. Currently, ICE possesses detention bedspace capacity for roughly 70,000 individuals and has considered plans to expand this capacity to over 90,000 in FY2026. 

 In contrast, the NDD refers to aliens who are subject to removal but are not detained . The docket includes individuals at any stage in the removal process . Individuals on the NDD remain under ICE supervision to help ensure that they regularly check in, comply with release conditions, attend court hearings, and comply with removal if so ordered. 

 The NDD Population

 Generally, the NDD population consists of aliens that 
 have been released at ICE's discretion following an initial or subsequent custody determination (as discussed previously); 

 are currently incarcerated in federal, state, and local facilities while serving sentences for criminal offenses; 

 have final removal orders but were granted temporary protection through withholding of removal or the Convention Against Torture (CAT) ;

 have final removal orders and are in the process of being repatriated; 

 have final removal orders but cannot be repatriated because their origin countries do not cooperate with the United States; 

 have final removal orders but absconded into the United States as fugitives ; and 

 unbeknownst to ICE, have voluntarily departed the United States or died and remain on the NDD erroneously. 
 ICE's most recently reported NDD population size of 7.3 million reflects its count of non-detained aliens as of February 26, 2026 ( Figure 1 ). All such individuals have been processed by ICE, including an estimated 1.6 million with final orders of removal . The NDD count relies on a cumulative list of removable aliens that is continuously updated; thus, it excludes those with a confirmed departure or death. Some aliens have been on the NDD for decades; others have been placed on it more recently. A fraction of NDD individuals are enrolled in ICE's Alternatives to Detention (ATD) program, which involves more intensive supervision than other NDD individuals who, in addition to attending all court hearings, typically must check in once a year with ICE. Currently, 180,000 individuals are on ATD.

 The NDD has more than tripled since FY2016 ( Figure 1 ). Recent NDD growth reflects high numbers of encounters (apprehensions) of aliens by the U.S. Border Patrol (USBP), part of DHS's Customs and Border Protection (CBP). From FY2016 through FY2020, annual USBP encounters at the Southwest border averaged about 470,000, and the NDD grew during that period from 2.2 million to 3.3 million unauthorized aliens. From FY2021 through FY2024, average annual encounters more than quadrupled to 1.9 million, boosting the NDD from 3.7 million to 7.7 million individuals. Since FY2025 (as of March 2026 ), USBP encounters have declined substantially. Increased ICE enforcement actions and removals that have prompted unauthorized aliens to self-deport have also reduced the NDD. Reportedly , about 72,000 aliens as of March 2026 have used a CBP incentive-based program to facilitate their voluntary departure and many others have left of their own accord.

 ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Statistics 

 ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Statistics

 U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) officers enforce immigration laws within the interior to preserve national security and public safety.

 ERO manages all aspects of the immigration enforcement process, including the identification, arrest, detention and removal of aliens who are subject to removal or are unlawfully present in the United States.

 Like all law enforcement agencies, ERO officers prioritize their enforcement actions based on agency and department priorities, funding and capacity. ERO operations are flexible enough to allow its officers to respond to events such as spikes in border crossings, modifications to U.S. laws, pandemics, and natural disasters at home and abroad.

 The following dashboards present for the first time information and trends in arrests, detentions, removals and alternatives to detention as of December 31, 2024. 

 The dashboards will be updated quarterly.

 "With the public release of this enforcement data, ICE is demonstrating its commitment to openness and transparency. We will continue to evaluate and enhance how the agency communicates measurable data to best inform how our officers and special agents perform their law enforcement missions in accordance with departmental and agency priorities.” — ICE Deputy Director and Senior Official Performing the Duties of the Director Patrick J. Lechleitner 

 --> 

 Arrest Statistics
 ERO enforces laws by arresting immigration violators in the interior of the United States. It relies on statutory law enforcement authority to identify and arrest aliens who may present threats to national security or public safety, or who otherwise undermine the integrity of U.S. immigration laws. ERO uses targeted, intelligence-driven operations to prioritize its enforcement actions in ways that help protect communities nationwide. While ERO primarily conducts administrative arrests of aliens it has probable cause to believe are removable from the United States, it also has the authority to execute criminal arrest warrants and initiate prosecutions for criminal activity, including immigration-related crimes. ERO officers assigned to task forces also help target and apprehend foreign fugitives in the United States who are wanted for crimes here and abroad by working with domestic and international partners.
 Arrests by country of citizenship and criminal history: ERO arrests are broken down by country of citizenship and categories of criminal history that include people with: U.S. criminal convictions.
 Pending criminal charges in the United States.
 No convictions or pending charges but who have broken U.S. immigration laws including visa overstays and Visa Waiver Program violators.*

*This category includes those who have repeatedly violated U.S. law by reentering after deportation, immigration fugitives with an executable final order of removal, and international fugitives wanted for crimes committed abroad.
 For fiscal years 2021 and 2022, this category also includes individuals apprehended while attempting to unlawfully enter the United States after January 1, 2021.

 ERO arrests over time: Historically, ERO most commonly arrests immigration violators with convictions involving DUI, drug possession, assault and criminal (non-civil) traffic offenses such as hit-and-run or leaving the scene of an accident.
 Arrests by Area of Responsibility (AOR): ERO has 24 field offices, which are geographic areas of responsibility , around the country, each headed by a field office director.

 Detention Statistics
 ERO oversees the civil immigration detention of one of the most diverse and rapidly changing detained populations in the world. The ERO Headquarters Custody Management and ICE Health Service Corps divisions help officers in the field manage the detained population and ensure detained aliens’ health and safety, ensure compliance with ICE’s detention standards, and provide medical care — including mental health care — to detained individuals.
 ICE detains individuals as necessary, including to secure their presence for immigration proceedings and removal from the United States. ICE also detains those who are subject to mandatory detention under U.S. immigration law and those a supervisor has determined are public safety or flight risks.
 After ICE arrests and processes individuals for administrative immigration violations or CBP and other state, local and federal law enforcement partners turn them over to ICE, officials may detain them while their immigration cases are pending or release them under a form of supervision. Both ICE and the Department of Justice’s Executive Office for Immigration Review — the office that oversees the immigration court system — can impact custody status at various points during a alien's immigration proceedings.
 Officials make custody determinations on an individual basis, taking into account all facets of a person’s situation, including their immigration history and criminal records. Authorities also consider family ties, humanitarian issues and whether a person may be a flight risk.
 Whenever possible, ICE seeks to house detained individuals within the geographical areas of their arrests to minimize their time in ICE custody and keep them close to family, friends and legal representatives.
 Most detained individuals are transfers from CBP following arrests at the border. ICE is legally obligated to detain some of these people, including those with certain criminal histories.
 If an alien or their representative believes they should not be subject to enforcement, detention or removal, they should contact their local ERO field office to request a case review or initiate the ICE Case Review process. People who want to contact ICE about their cases should first notify their local ERO field office via email with supporting documentation for an initial review.

 Individuals with pending criminal charges.

Word count: brief.md 1,200–1,600 words. Structure per Brief 13 format:
- Title (title case, headline)
- Executive summary (3 bullets)
- Body sections 1–4
- Recommendations (3-5, imperative, addressed to Congress)
- Byline: Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy

Wait — the deliverable says "by Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy." Yes.

Style sheet rules:
- A1: AP style; headlines in title case; no em-dash runs. So avoid em dashes. Use commas/colons/parentheses. I must avoid "—" runs. I'll avoid em dashes entirely.
- A2: "illegal alien" in body copy; "noncitizen" when quoting federal data that uses it.
- A3: Lead with public safety and victims; persuasive, not "on the one hand".
- A4: Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.
- B1: every figure carries its source and date. Hmm — "Every figure carries its source and date." That means in the body copy, figures should carry source and date. Hmm, that's a bit unusual but it's the style sheet. In the published Brief 13 format, the appendix carries "Source: ...". Hmm, but B1 says "Every figure carries its source and date. Population, timeframe and methodology notes go in the appendix notes, not in body copy, the fact sheet or cards." So: body copy figures should be attributed inline (e.g., "according to ICE data reported to Congress in September 2024") with dates, but the methodological detail goes to the appendix. I'll attribute inline concisely with dates for each figure in the body, and full source lines in the appendix.
- B2: prefer federal primary sources.
- B3: Cato in appendix only, one line, followed by CIS critique.
- B4: charts — not needed for markdown deliverables, but maybe mention chart specs? The deliverables don't include charts. I'll skip. Actually, maybe I should note in the appendix the chart colors for the design team? Not required. Skip, or a small note. I'll add a "Chart note" in the appendix for the tables that might become charts — this shows attention to B4 without overdoing it. Actually, the appendix says "publication-ready tables with source lines and notes, one table per figure used in the brief." I'll include a chart spec line for one or two tables where a chart would be natural, e.g., "Chart: FSI navy #1F3A5F bars, y-axis from zero." That's a nice touch demonstrating style compliance. I'll add a brief "Chart spec" note for a couple of tables. Keep it light.
- C1: source line format: Agency/author, Title, Date, URL.
- C2: fact sheet every stat footnoted.

Now: ethics. The brief must be persuasive but honest. Key risk areas:

1. The 13,099 figure. I must present it accurately: "noncitizens with homicide convictions on ICE's non-detained docket as of 21 July 2024." I will not say they are "free" or "roaming the streets" (many are in state/federal prisons). Per B1, the timeframe and methodology notes go in the appendix notes — I'll include: DHS statements that records go back four decades, that the docket includes noncitizens currently incarcerated by other authorities, that ICE has not said how many, and that the docket includes legally admitted noncitizens. This is the key honesty safeguard, and it's required by B1 (notes in appendix) and it's in the source table's own "Context" line, so the author expects it.

2. The USSC 34.7% figure. Must present accurately: noncitizens were 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024, and 88.7% of those were illegal aliens; most (72.3%) were sentenced for immigration offenses. The persuasive framing: "more than a third of everyone sentenced in federal court in FY2024 was not a U.S. citizen." That's accurate. I should be careful with "88.7% were illegal aliens" — that's the USSC's own terminology. Fine to cite.

Also the GAO 27% decline — that's a counter-fact for the argument (fewer noncitizens sentenced). Why would the author include it? Probably to show... hmm. Actually, it could cut against "criminal aliens are flooding the courts." I'll use it carefully or leave it to the appendix. Actually, it's in the source table T2, so the research assistant included it. Where does it fit? It could be framed as: "Even as the number of noncitizens sentenced in federal court fell 27 percent between FY2018 and FY2023, noncitizens still accounted for more than a third of all federal sentences in FY2024." Hmm, that's awkward. Or in the context of the appendix. I think I'll include it in the appendix table as context, and possibly one line in the body. Actually, including it in the body is honest and preempts the counter-argument... but the style sheet says lead with the powerful numbers. I'll include it in the appendix only, and note in notes_for_reviewers that the GAO decline figure is in the appendix for completeness. Hmm, but wait — is there a legitimate persuasive use? Yes: it shows that the decline tracks the decline in border enforcement... no, actually it tracks fewer prosecutions. I'll keep it in the appendix as context with a note. Actually, let me reconsider: the brief's credibility benefits from one line acknowledging it. I'll put a single clause in the body: "GAO finds the number of noncitizens sentenced in federal court fell 27 percent from FY2018 to FY2023, but the share of federal sentences imposed on noncitizens remains more than one in three." That's honest and still on-message. I'll include it — it's accurate and preempts a rebuttal. Hmm, but the system prompt says keep caveats out. The style sheet governs, and the style sheet doesn't forbid caveats in body copy; it only confines *methodology notes* to the appendix and *counter-research* to the appendix. A factual trend line from GAO is not counter-research per se (it's from T2, the author's own source table). I'll include a brief mention in the body with the appendix carrying it. Good balance.

3. Texas section. The body should present CIS's reading of Texas DPS data with attribution, and be careful not to overstate: CIS says "the DPS data suggests that illegal immigrants in Texas are convicted of homicide and sexual assault at higher rates than the state average. Significant uncertainties remain, however, especially regarding lesser offenses." I'll characterize it accurately: "When Texas's delayed identification of offenders is taken into account, CIS's reanalysis of the same DPS data finds illegal immigrants are convicted of homicide and sexual assault at higher rates than the state average." And the appendix carries the Cato one-liner + CIS critique per B3. I must be careful in the body not to claim certainty beyond what CIS claims. Also I should attribute it to CIS by name — a think tank analysis, not federal primary data. B2 says prefer federal primary sources, but Texas DPS is state. I'll note the data source is Texas DPS and the analysis is CIS.

Actually, important: is it fair to present CIS's contested analysis in the body without noting it's disputed? The style sheet explicitly mandates this structure (B3), so the Director has made that editorial call. I'll follow it but make attribution crystal clear ("a Center for Immigration Studies reanalysis") so the reader knows whose finding it is. And the appendix will present both Cato and CIS. That's a defensible, transparent approach. I'll also flag in notes_for_reviewers that section 3 rests on contested analyses and suggest the editor may want to strengthen the framing.

4. The New York numbers from DHS press releases — these are federal primary sources but advocacy-toned. I'll use the counts with attribution and date. The 6,947 released criminal illegal aliens figure is a DHS/ICE claim; I'll attribute precisely: "DHS reported in December 2025 that New York's failure to honor ICE detainers had resulted in the release of 6,947 criminal illegal aliens since January 20, 2025, and that their offenses included 29 homicides."

Also the 148 homicides among 7,113 aliens currently in NY custody with active detainers. Good, powerful, dated, attributed.

5. The 41,085 declined detainers — attribute to House Judiciary Committee citing ICE information, Oct 2022–early 2026.

6. Laken Riley — brief mention per the outline's instruction ("fine to mention briefly; do not invent others"). Facts: Aug. 22, 2024? No — Feb. 22, 2024. Convicted Nov 20, 2024, life without parole. Ibarra entered illegally Sept 2022 near El Paso, paroled; NYPD arrest Aug 31, 2023 released before ICE could lodge detainer. I'll write it briefly and accurately.

- Dates: AP style uses "Sept. 25, 2024" abbreviations for months in dates (Jan., Feb., Aug., Sept., Oct., Nov., Dec.). I'll use AP-style dates in body copy ("Sept. 25, 2024") and a consistent compact date in source lines ("25 Sep 2024") — hmm, mixed formats might be inconsistent. Let me use AP style everywhere in body copy ("Sept. 25, 2024") and in source lines use the same AP style to be consistent: "ICE (Patrick J. Lechleitner, Acting Director), Letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, Sept. 25, 2024, https://...". That's cleaner and AP-consistent. The style sheet itself writes "Jun 2026" but that's the style sheet's own header. I'll go AP.

- Numbers: AP spells out one through nine, numerals for 10+. Percent: AP uses "%" with numerals in data-heavy copy? AP style is "34.7 percent" in text, though newer AP allows "%" in headlines/tables. FSI series uses "34.7%". I'll use "%" in tables/cards and "percent" in body prose... Hmm. Actually for a data-heavy policy brief, "%" is fine and cleaner. AP's 2019 update: use "%" with a numeral. Yes, AP now permits "%" with numerals. I'll use "%" consistently.

- "illegal alien" statutory term. Note 8 U.S.C. 1365 defines "illegal alien". Good, mentioned in A2.

- No em dashes. I'll use commas, colons, parentheses.

- Titles: "Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14: Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show" — the given title. Headline in title case: "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show".

{"path": "/workspace/out/brief.md", "content": "# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**

By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy

Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.

Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

*DRAFT FOR EDITORIAL REVIEW. Not for distribution.*

## Executive summary

- ICE reported to Congress that 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on the agency's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, inside a population of 425,431 convicted criminals ICE was not holding. Convictions in that population also included 15,811 sexual assaults, 62,231 assaults, 56,533 dangerous drug offenses and 13,423 weapons offenses.
- Noncitizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in U.S. district court in fiscal 2024, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission.
- Between October 2022 and early 2026, sanctuary jurisdictions declined at least 41,085 ICE detainers. New York alone released 6,947 criminal illegal aliens rather than transfer them to ICE during 2025, and their offenses included 29 homicides.

## Enforcement that arrives after the victim

On Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered on a running trail at the University of Georgia. The man convicted of killing her, Jose Antonio Ibarra, had entered the United States illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was paroled into the country. In August 2023 the New York Police Department arrested him on a charge of acting in a manner injurious to a child. He walked out of local custody before ICE could lodge a detainer. Six months later he was in Athens, Georgia. A judge sentenced him to life without parole in November 2024.

The federal government's own records describe that sequence in the aggregate, at scale. The data reviewed in this brief, from ICE, the Sentencing Commission, GAO and the Congressional Research Service, show a public safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement that Congress has the tools to reduce and has so far declined to use.

## 1. Criminal aliens the government knows about and does not hold

ICE's numbers are not estimates. They are the agency's own case counts, reported to Congress.

As of July 21, 2024, ICE's national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories: 435,719 convicted criminals and 226,847 with pending criminal charges. The majority of the convicted, 425,431 people, sat on the non-detained docket, which means ICE was not holding them when the count was taken. Their conviction records included 13,099 homicides, 15,811 sexual assaults, 62,231 assaults, 56,533 dangerous drug offenses and 13,423 weapons offenses. A further 1,845 noncitizens on that docket faced pending homicide charges.

The docket behind those numbers has grown faster than any enforcement response to it. CRS reported in April 2026 that the non-detained docket stood at 7.3 million aliens as of Feb. 26, 2026, more than triple its fiscal 2016 size, and that roughly 1.6 million of those aliens already hold final orders of removal. ICE supervises that population with about 70,000 beds of detention capacity and reported 66,978 people in custody on April 9, 2026. Expansion beyond 90,000 beds remains, in CRS's phrasing, a plan under consideration rather than an appropriation.

That is the arithmetic of the problem. Mandatory detention under section 236 of the Immigration and Nationality Act is only as real as the bed behind it, and Congress funds the beds.

## 2. One in three federal sentences

In fiscal 2024, U.S. district courts sentenced 61,678 individuals. The Sentencing Commission reports that 21,304 of them, 34.7%, were not U.S. citizens, and that 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. Immigration was the leading guideline under which noncitizens were sentenced, at 72.3%, followed by drug trafficking at 17.6%.

GAO's review of the same docket found the number of noncitizens sentenced in federal court fell 27% between fiscal 2018 and fiscal 2023, from roughly 29,500 to roughly 21,500, and that about 76% of noncitizens sentenced over that period were sentenced for immigration offenses. Even after that decline, noncitizens still accounted for more than a third of all federal sentences in fiscal 2024. The federal criminal caseload tracks the border: when entry is unenforced, the resulting cases arrive in federal court, and in immigration detention, and in the communities where released offenders settle.

## 3. What the state evidence shows

Texas is the only state that records the immigration status of everyone it arrests and convicts, which makes its Department of Public Safety data the best available state-level check on the federal picture. The direction of those numbers turns on one methodological choice: whether an offender is counted as an illegal alien when Texas first records the case, or only after the state completes a status check that can take years of custody to finish.

Read the first way, illegal immigrants appear less criminally active than the native-born. Read the second way, and accounting for offenders Texas identifies only after incarceration, illegal immigrants are convicted of homicide and sexual assault at rates above the state average, as a Center for Immigration Studies reanalysis of DPS conviction data concludes. The competing readings, and the reasons for the disagreement, are set out in the appendix to this brief.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and the detainer problem

A detainer is the cheapest transfer in American law enforcement. The alien is already in local custody; ICE asks only to be told before he is released, and to hold him for up to 48 hours while a federal officer drives to the jail.

Between October 2022 and early 2026, sanctuary jurisdictions declined at least 41,085 of those requests, according to ICE information reported by the House Judiciary Committee.

New York is the case study. In December 2025, DHS reported that the state's failure to honor detainers had freed 6,947 criminal illegal aliens since Jan. 20, 2025, and that their offenses included 29 homicides, 2,509 assaults, 305 robberies and 207 sexual predator offenses. In February 2026, DHS counted 7,113 aliens in New York custody with active detainers, 148 of them with homicide offenses. Every one of those people is a known quantity to two governments, and one of them refuses the handoff.

Where local agencies do cooperate, the results are measurable. ICE held 2,246 active 287(g) agreements as of Aug. 1, 2026, an increase of 1,564% since Jan. 20, 2025. Cooperation is a policy choice. So is refusal.

## Recommendations

Congress should:

1. **Fund detention for the criminal non-detained docket.** Appropriate capacity above 90,000 beds and direct DHS to fill those beds first with aliens convicted of or charged with homicide, sexual assault, other violent offenses, drug trafficking and firearms offenses. A docket of 7.3 million aliens cannot be supervised with 70,000 beds, and the violent subset of that docket should never wait behind a queue of noncriminal cases.

2. **Make detainer compliance a condition of federal law enforcement funding.** Withhold discretionary grant funds from jurisdictions that decline ICE detainers, and codify a right of action for victims of crimes committed by aliens released after a detainer was declined.

3. **Codify and fund the 287(g) program.** Place the jail enforcement, task force and warrant service officer models in statute rather than leave them to executive discretion, appropriate training funds for participating agencies, and require quarterly reporting of arrests and removals attributable to the program.

4. **Require DHS to publish what it releases.** Put the Declined Detainer Outcome Report back in statute and require quarterly publication of the criminal conviction profile of the non-detained docket, so that a figure like 13,099 surfaces on schedule rather than only in response to a congressional letter.

5. **Close the gaps in mandatory detention.** Extend mandatory detention to any alien convicted of a crime of violence or a sexual offense, extending the principle Congress enacted in the Laken Riley Act beyond theft, burglary and assault on officers.

The data reviewed here are the government's own. They describe a system that identifies offenders, in many cases convicts them, and then releases them into the communities that Congress is sworn to protect. That is not an argument about the border in the abstract. It is a count of the cost, and it is available to any member of Congress who asks.

---

*Brett Kessler is Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy at the Founders' Square Institute. Data appendix available at fsi.org. "Illegal alien" is the statutory term at 8 U.S.C. 1365; "noncitizen" is used where it is the federal data term.*

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14 | Founders' Square Institute | Oct. 27, 2026**

*For Hill offices. One page. All figures are agency data; source lines below.*

## The numbers

**13,099** noncitizens with homicide convictions were on ICE's non-detained docket, meaning not in ICE custody, as of July 21, 2024.[1]

**425,431** convicted criminals were on that same non-detained docket, with convictions including 15,811 sexual assaults, 62,231 assaults, 56,533 dangerous drug offenses and 13,423 weapons offenses.[1]

**7.3 million** aliens were on ICE's non-detained docket as of Feb. 26, 2026, about 1.6 million of them with final orders of removal. ICE holds roughly 70,000 detention beds and reported 66,978 people in custody on April 9, 2026.[2]

**34.7%** of all individuals sentenced in U.S. district court in fiscal 2024, 21,304 of 61,678, were not U.S. citizens. **88.7%** of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.[3]

**41,085** ICE detainers were declined by sanctuary jurisdictions between October 2022 and early 2026, per ICE information reported by the House Judiciary Committee.[4]

**2,246** active 287(g) cooperation agreements were in force as of Aug. 1, 2026, an increase of 1,564% since Jan. 20, 2025.[6]

Contact: FSI Office of Communications, media@fsi.org, (202) 555-0100

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

## New FSI Brief: ICE Was Holding None of 13,099 Noncitizens With Homicide Convictions

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026: The Founders' Square Institute today published Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy. The brief assembles federal data on criminal aliens released into American communities and sets out five actions for Congress.

ICE reported to Congress that 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on the agency's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, inside a population of 425,431 convicted criminals ICE was not holding. Their records included 15,811 sexual assault convictions, 62,231 assault convictions and 13,423 weapons convictions. The non-detained docket now stands at 7.3 million aliens, against roughly 70,000 beds of ICE detention capacity.

The brief also documents at least 41,085 ICE detainers declined by sanctuary jurisdictions between October 2022 and early 2026, and 6,947 criminal illegal aliens released by New York during 2025 rather than transferred to ICE, including 29 with homicide offenses.

"These are the government's own numbers, not estimates and not advocacy," Kessler said. "ICE has identified more than 425,000 convicted criminals it is not holding, more than 13,000 of them with homicide convictions, and it is supervising a docket of 7.3 million people with about 70,000 beds. Congress funds those beds and writes the detention statutes. Neither has kept pace, and the difference is measured in victims. Our recommendations are actionable this Congress: fund the beds, enforce detainer compliance, put 287(g) in statute, and make DHS report what it releases."

The brief recommends that Congress appropriate detention capacity above 90,000 beds and direct DHS to fill them first with aliens convicted of violent and sexual offenses; condition federal law enforcement grants on detainer compliance; codify and fund the 287(g) program, now at 2,246 active agreements; require quarterly publication of the criminal profile of the non-detained docket; and extend mandatory detention to aliens convicted of crimes of violence and sexual offenses.

The Founders' Square Institute is a nonpartisan public-policy think tank in Washington, D.C. Brief No. 14, with a full data appendix and a one-page fact sheet for Hill offices, is available at fsi.org.

###

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**

By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy

Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.

Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

*DRAFT FOR EDITORIAL REVIEW. Not for distribution.*

## Executive summary

- ICE reported to Congress that 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on the agency's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, inside a population of 425,431 convicted criminals ICE was not holding. Convictions in that population also included 15,811 sexual assaults, 62,231 assaults, 56,533 dangerous drug offenses and 13,423 weapons offenses.
- Noncitizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in U.S. district court in fiscal 2024, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission.
- Between October 2022 and early 2026, sanctuary jurisdictions declined at least 41,085 ICE detainers, per ICE information reported by the House Judiciary Committee. New York alone released 6,947 criminal illegal aliens rather than transfer them to ICE during 2025, and their offenses included 29 homicides.

## Enforcement that arrives after the victim

On Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered on a running trail at the University of Georgia. The man convicted of killing her, Jose Antonio Ibarra, had entered the United States illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was paroled into the country. In August 2023 the New York Police Department arrested him on a charge of acting in a manner injurious to a child. He walked out of local custody before ICE could lodge a detainer. Six months later he was in Athens, Georgia. A judge sentenced him to life without parole in November 2024.

The federal government's own records describe that sequence in the aggregate, at scale. The data reviewed in this brief, from ICE, the Sentencing Commission, GAO and the Congressional Research Service, show a public safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement that Congress has the tools to reduce and has so far declined to use.

## 1. Criminal aliens the government knows about and does not hold

ICE's numbers are not estimates. They are the agency's own case counts, reported to Congress.

As of July 21, 2024, ICE's national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories: 435,719 convicted criminals and 226,847 with pending criminal charges. The majority of the convicted, 425,431 people, sat on the non-detained docket, which means ICE was not holding them when the count was taken. Their conviction records included 13,099 homicides, 15,811 sexual assaults, 62,231 assaults, 56,533 dangerous drug offenses and 13,423 weapons offenses. A further 1,845 noncitizens on that docket faced pending homicide charges.

The docket behind those numbers has grown faster than any enforcement response to it. CRS reported in April 2026 that the non-detained docket stood at 7.3 million aliens as of Feb. 26, 2026, more than triple its fiscal 2016 size, and that roughly 1.6 million of those aliens already hold final orders of removal. ICE supervises that population with about 70,000 beds of detention capacity and reported 66,978 people in custody on April 9, 2026. CRS reports that ICE has considered plans to expand bedspace to more than 90,000 in fiscal 2026, which as of the April 2026 report was a plan rather than an appropriation.

That is the arithmetic of the problem. Mandatory detention under section 236 of the Immigration and Nationality Act is only as real as the bed behind it, and Congress funds the beds.

## 2. One in three federal sentences

In fiscal 2024, U.S. district courts sentenced 61,678 individuals. The Sentencing Commission reports that 21,304 of them, 34.7%, were not U.S. citizens, and that 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. Immigration was the leading guideline under which noncitizens were sentenced, at 72.3%, followed by drug trafficking at 17.6%.

GAO's review of the same docket found the number of noncitizens sentenced in federal court fell 27% between fiscal 2018 and fiscal 2023, from roughly 29,500 to roughly 21,500, and that about 76% of noncitizens sentenced over that period were sentenced for immigration offenses. Even after that decline, noncitizens still accounted for more than a third of all federal sentences in fiscal 2024. The federal criminal caseload tracks the border: when entry is unenforced, the resulting cases arrive in federal court, and in immigration detention, and in the communities where released offenders settle.

## 3. What the state evidence shows

Texas is the only state that records the immigration status of everyone it arrests and convicts, which makes its Department of Public Safety data the best available state-level check on the federal picture. The two readings of that dataset diverge on a single choice: whether an offender is counted as an illegal alien when Texas first records the case, or only after the state completes a status check that can require years of custody to finish.

Counted at the point of first processing, illegal aliens in Texas have a lower homicide conviction rate than native-born Americans. Counted once Texas has finished identifying offenders in custody, illegal aliens are convicted of homicide and sexual assault at rates above the state average, as a 2022 Center for Immigration Studies reanalysis of DPS conviction data concludes. Both readings, and the reasons for the disagreement, are documented in the appendix to this brief.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and the detainer problem

A detainer is the cheapest transfer in American law enforcement. The alien is already in local custody; ICE asks only to be told before he is released, and to hold him for up to 48 hours while a federal officer drives to the jail.

Between October 2022 and early 2026, sanctuary jurisdictions declined at least 41,085 of those requests, according to ICE information reported by the House Judiciary Committee.

New York is the case study. In December 2025, DHS reported that the state's failure to honor detainers had freed 6,947 criminal illegal aliens since Jan. 20, 2025, and that their offenses included 29 homicides, 2,509 assaults, 305 robberies and 207 sexual predator offenses. In February 2026, DHS counted 7,113 aliens in New York custody with active detainers, 148 of them with homicide offenses. Every one of those people is a known quantity to two governments, and one of them refuses the handoff.

Where local agencies do cooperate, the results are measurable. ICE held 2,246 active 287(g) agreements as of Aug. 1, 2026, an increase of 1,564% since Jan. 20, 2025. Cooperation is a policy choice. So is refusal.

## Recommendations

Congress should:

1. **Fund detention for the criminal non-detained docket.** Appropriate capacity above 90,000 beds and direct DHS to fill those beds first with aliens convicted of or charged with homicide, sexual assault, other violent offenses, drug trafficking and firearms offenses. A docket of 7.3 million aliens cannot be supervised with 70,000 beds, and the violent subset of that docket should never wait behind a queue of noncriminal cases.

2. **Make detainer compliance a condition of federal law enforcement funding.** Withhold discretionary grant funds from jurisdictions that decline ICE detainers, and codify a right of action for victims of crimes committed by aliens released after a detainer was declined.

3. **Codify and fund the 287(g) program.** Place the jail enforcement, task force and warrant service officer models in statute rather than leave them to executive discretion, appropriate training funds for participating agencies, and require quarterly reporting of arrests and removals attributable to the program.

4. **Require DHS to publish what it releases.** Put the Declined Detainer Outcome Report back in statute and require quarterly publication of the criminal conviction profile of the non-detained docket, so that a figure like 13,099 surfaces on schedule rather than only in response to a congressional letter.

5. **Close the gaps in mandatory detention.** Extend mandatory detention to any alien convicted of a crime of violence or a sexual offense, extending the principle Congress enacted in the Laken Riley Act beyond theft, burglary and assault on officers.

The data reviewed here are the government's own. They describe a system that identifies offenders, in many cases convicts them, and then releases them into the communities that Congress is sworn to protect. That is not an argument about the border in the abstract. It is a count of the cost, and it is available to any member of Congress who asks.

---

*Brett Kessler is Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy at the Founders' Square Institute. Data appendix available at fsi.org. "Illegal alien" is the statutory term at 8 U.S.C. 1365; "noncitizen" is used where it is the federal data term.*

# FACT SHEET: Criminal Aliens and Public Safety, What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14 | Founders' Square Institute | Oct. 27, 2026**

*For Hill offices. One page. All figures are agency data; source lines below.*

## The numbers

**13,099** noncitizens with homicide convictions were on ICE's non-detained docket, meaning not in ICE custody, as of July 21, 2024.[1]

**425,431** convicted criminals were on that same non-detained docket, with convictions including 15,811 sexual assaults, 62,231 assaults, 56,533 dangerous drug offenses and 13,423 weapons offenses.[1]

**7.3 million** aliens were on ICE's non-detained docket as of Feb. 26, 2026, about 1.6 million of them with final orders of removal. ICE holds roughly 70,000 detention beds and reported 66,978 people in custody on April 9, 2026.[2]

**34.7%** of all individuals sentenced in U.S. district court in fiscal 2024, 21,304 of 61,678, were not U.S. citizens. **88.7%** of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.[3]

**41,085** ICE detainers were declined by sanctuary jurisdictions between October 2022 and early 2026, per ICE information reported by the House Judiciary Committee.[4]

**6,947** criminal illegal aliens were released by New York rather than transferred to ICE between Jan. 20, 2025 and Dec. 1, 2025, and their offenses included 29 homicides. As of Feb. 6, 2026, 7,113 aliens with active detainers were in New York custody, 148 with homicide offenses.[5]

**2,246** active 287(g) cooperation agreements were in force as of Aug. 1, 2026, an increase of 1,564% since Jan. 20, 2025.[6]

**72.3%** of noncitizens sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024 were sentenced under the immigration guideline, followed by drug trafficking at 17.6%.[3]

## What Congress can do

Appropriate detention capacity above 90,000 beds and direct DHS to fill them first with aliens convicted of violent and sexual offenses. Condition federal law enforcement grants on detainer compliance. Codify and fund 287(g). Require DHS to publish the criminal profile of the non-detained docket and every declined detainer each quarter.

## Sources

1. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (Patrick J. Lechleitner, Acting Director), Letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, Sept. 25, 2024, https://homeland.house.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/24-01143-ICEs-Signed-Response-to-Representative-Tony-Gonzales.pdf. Offense counts as of July 21, 2024.
2. Congressional Research Service, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Non-Detained Docket (NDD), IF13208, April 24, 2026, https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/IF/PDF/IF13208/IF13208.1.pdf.
3. U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Federally Sentenced Non-U.S. Citizens, FY2024, https://www.ussc.gov/sites/default/files/pdf/research-and-publications/quick-facts/Non-Citizen_FY24.pdf.
4. U.S. House of Representatives, Report 119-541, Shut Down Sanctuary Policies Act of 2026, March 12, 2026, https://www.congress.gov/committee-report/119th-congress/house-report/541/1.
5. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Sanctuary New York Released Nearly 7,000 Criminal Illegal Aliens, Dec. 1, 2025, https://www.dhs.gov/news/2025/12/01/sanctuary-new-york-released-nearly-7000-criminal-illegal-aliens-including-murderers; U.S. Department of Homeland Security, DHS Calls on Mamdani to Not Release Criminal Illegal Aliens From New York City's Custody, Feb. 6, 2026, https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/02/06/dhs-calls-mamdani-not-release-criminal-illegal-aliens-new-york-citys-custody.
6. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, 287(g) Fact Sheet, July 2026, data as of Aug. 1, 2026, https://www.ice.gov/doclib/about/offices/ero/287g/factsheet287g.pdf.

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**

By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy

Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.

Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

*DRAFT FOR EDITORIAL REVIEW. Not for distribution.*

## Executive summary

- ICE reported to Congress that 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on the agency's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, inside a population of 425,431 convicted criminals ICE was not holding. Convictions in that population also included 15,811 sexual assaults, 62,231 assaults, 56,533 dangerous drug offenses and 13,423 weapons offenses.
- Noncitizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in U.S. district court in fiscal 2024, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission.
- Between October 2022 and early 2026, sanctuary jurisdictions declined at least 41,085 ICE detainers, per ICE information reported by the House Judiciary Committee. New York alone released 6,947 criminal illegal aliens rather than transfer them to ICE during 2025, and their offenses included 29 homicides.

## Enforcement that arrives after the victim

On Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered on a running trail at the University of Georgia in Athens. The man convicted of killing her, Jose Antonio Ibarra, had entered the United States illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was paroled into the country. In August 2023 the New York Police Department arrested him on a charge of acting in a manner injurious to a child. He was released before ICE could lodge a detainer. Less than six months after that release, Laken Riley was dead. A judge sentenced Ibarra to life without parole in November 2024.

The federal government's own records describe that sequence in the aggregate, at scale. The data reviewed in this brief, from ICE, the Sentencing Commission, GAO and the Congressional Research Service, show a public safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement that Congress has the tools to reduce and has so far declined to use.

## 1. Criminal aliens the government knows about and does not hold

ICE's numbers are not estimates. They are the agency's own case counts, reported to Congress.

As of July 21, 2024, ICE's national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories: 435,719 convicted criminals and 226,847 with pending criminal charges. The majority of the convicted, 425,431 people, sat on the non-detained docket, which means ICE was not holding them when the count was taken. Their conviction records included 13,099 homicides, 15,811 sexual assaults, 62,231 assaults, 56,533 dangerous drug offenses and 13,423 weapons offenses. A further 1,845 noncitizens on that docket faced pending homicide charges.

The docket behind those numbers has grown faster than any enforcement response to it. CRS reported in April 2026 that the non-detained docket stood at 7.3 million aliens as of Feb. 26, 2026, more than triple its fiscal 2016 size, and that roughly 1.6 million of those aliens already hold final orders of removal. ICE supervises that population with about 70,000 beds of detention capacity and reported 66,978 people in custody on April 9, 2026. CRS reports that ICE has considered plans to expand bedspace to more than 90,000 in fiscal 2026, which as of the April 2026 report was a plan rather than an appropriation.

That is the arithmetic of the problem. Mandatory detention under section 236 of the Immigration and Nationality Act is only as real as the bed behind it, and Congress funds the beds.

## 2. One in three federal sentences

In fiscal 2024, U.S. district courts sentenced 61,678 individuals. The Sentencing Commission reports that 21,304 of them, 34.7%, were not U.S. citizens, and that 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. Immigration was the leading guideline under which noncitizens were sentenced, at 72.3%, followed by drug trafficking at 17.6%.

GAO's review of the same docket found the number of noncitizens sentenced in federal court fell 27% between fiscal 2018 and fiscal 2023, from roughly 29,500 to roughly 21,500, and that about 76% of noncitizens sentenced over that period were sentenced for immigration offenses. Even after that decline, noncitizens still accounted for more than a third of all federal sentences in fiscal 2024. The federal criminal caseload tracks the border. When entry goes unenforced, the resulting cases arrive in federal court, in immigration detention and in the communities where released offenders settle.

## 3. What the state evidence shows

Texas is the only state that records the immigration status of everyone it arrests and convicts, which makes its Department of Public Safety data the best available state-level check on the federal picture. The two readings of that dataset diverge on a single choice: whether an offender is counted as an illegal alien when Texas first records the case, or only after the state completes a status check that can require years of custody to finish.

Counted at the point of first processing, illegal aliens in Texas have a lower homicide conviction rate than native-born Americans. Counted once Texas has finished identifying offenders in custody, illegal aliens are convicted of homicide and sexual assault at rates above the state average, as a 2022 Center for Immigration Studies reanalysis of DPS conviction data concludes. Both readings, and the reasons for the disagreement, are documented in the appendix to this brief.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and the detainer problem

A detainer is the cheapest transfer in American law enforcement. The alien is already in local custody; ICE asks only to be told before he is released, and to hold him for up to 48 hours while a federal officer drives to the jail.

Between October 2022 and early 2026, sanctuary jurisdictions declined at least 41,085 of those requests, according to ICE information reported by the House Judiciary Committee.

New York is the case study. In December 2025, DHS reported that the state's failure to honor detainers had freed 6,947 criminal illegal aliens since Jan. 20, 2025, and that their offenses included 29 homicides, 2,509 assaults, 305 robberies and 207 sexual predator offenses. In February 2026, DHS counted 7,113 aliens in New York custody with active detainers, 148 of them with homicide offenses. Every one of those people is a known quantity to two governments, and one of them refuses the handoff.

Where local agencies do cooperate, the results are measurable. ICE held 2,246 active 287(g) agreements as of Aug. 1, 2026, an increase of 1,564% since Jan. 20, 2025. Cooperation is a policy choice. So is refusal.

## Recommendations

Congress should:

1. **Fund detention for the criminal non-detained docket.** Appropriate capacity above 90,000 beds and direct DHS to fill those beds first with aliens convicted of or charged with homicide, sexual assault, other violent offenses, drug trafficking and firearms offenses. A docket of 7.3 million aliens cannot be supervised with 70,000 beds, and the violent subset of that docket should never wait behind a queue of noncriminal cases.

2. **Make detainer compliance a condition of federal law enforcement funding.** Withhold discretionary grant funds from jurisdictions that decline ICE detainers, and codify a right of action for victims of crimes committed by aliens released after a detainer was declined.

3. **Codify and fund the 287(g) program.** Place the jail enforcement, task force and warrant service officer models in statute rather than leave them to executive discretion, appropriate training funds for participating agencies, and require quarterly reporting of arrests and removals attributable to the program.

4. **Require DHS to publish what it releases.** Put the Declined Detainer Outcome Report back in statute and require quarterly publication of the criminal conviction profile of the non-detained docket, so that a figure like 13,099 surfaces on schedule rather than only in response to a congressional letter.

5. **Close the gaps in mandatory detention.** Extend mandatory detention to any alien convicted of a crime of violence or a sexual offense, extending the principle Congress enacted in the Laken Riley Act beyond theft, burglary and assault on officers.

The data reviewed here are the government's own. They describe a system that identifies offenders, in many cases convicts them, and then releases them into the communities that Congress is sworn to protect. That is not an argument about the border in the abstract. It is a count of the cost, and it is available to any member of Congress who asks.

---

*Brett Kessler is Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy at the Founders' Square Institute. Data appendix available at fsi.org. "Illegal alien" is the statutory term at 8 U.S.C. 1365; "noncitizen" is used where it is the federal data term.*

U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Sanctuary New York Released Nearly 7,000 Criminal Illegal Aliens Including Murderers, Terrorists, and Sexual Predators, Dec. 1, 2025, https://www.dhs.gov/news/2025/12/01/sanctuary-new-york-released-nearly-7000-criminal-illegal-aliens-including-murderers. A detainer is a request that a local agency hold a removable alien up to 48 hours beyond release and notify ICE before release. The Ibarra case: Jose Antonio Ibarra entered illegally near El Paso on Sept. 8, 2022 and was paroled; the New York Police Department arrested him on Aug. 31, 2023 and he was released before ICE lodged a detainer; he was convicted of the murder of Laken Riley in Athens, Georgia, on Nov. 20, 2024 and sentenced to life without parole. "Illegal alien" is the statutory term at 8 U.S.C. 1365 and is used in FSI body copy. "Noncitizen" is used where it is the term used by the federal dataset being cited, principally ICE and the Sentencing Commission.

# FACT SHEET: Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14 | Founders' Square Institute | Oct. 27, 2026**

*For Hill offices. One page. Every figure is footnoted; full notes in the brief's data appendix.*

## The numbers

**13,099** noncitizens with homicide convictions were on ICE's non-detained docket, meaning not in ICE custody, as of July 21, 2024.[1]

**425,431** convicted criminals were on that same non-detained docket, with convictions including 15,811 sexual assaults, 62,231 assaults, 56,533 dangerous drug offenses and 13,423 weapons offenses.[1]

**7.3 million** aliens were on ICE's non-detained docket as of Feb. 26, 2026, about 1.6 million of them with final orders of removal. ICE holds roughly 70,000 detention beds and reported 66,978 people in custody on April 9, 2026.[2]

**34.7%** of all individuals sentenced in U.S. district court in fiscal 2024, 21,304 of 61,678, were not U.S. citizens. **88.7%** of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.[3]

**72.3%** of noncitizens sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024 were sentenced under the immigration guideline, followed by drug trafficking at 17.6%.[3]

**41,085** ICE detainers were declined by sanctuary jurisdictions between October 2022 and early 2026, per ICE information reported by the House Judiciary Committee.[4]

**6,947** criminal illegal aliens were released by New York rather than transferred to ICE between Jan. 20, 2025 and Dec. 1, 2025, and their offenses included 29 homicides. As of Feb. 6, 2026, 7,113 aliens with active detainers were in New York custody, 148 with homicide offenses.[5]

**2,246** active 287(g) cooperation agreements were in force as of Aug. 1, 2026, an increase of 1,564% since Jan. 20, 2025.[6]

## What Congress can do

Appropriate detention capacity above 90,000 beds and direct DHS to fill them first with aliens convicted of violent and sexual offenses. Condition federal law enforcement grants on detainer compliance. Codify and fund 287(g). Require DHS to publish the criminal profile of the non-detained docket and every declined detainer each quarter.

EMBARGOED UNTIL TUESDAY, OCT. 27, 2026, 10:00 A.M. ET

Contact: FSI Office of Communications, media@fsi.org, (202) 555-0100

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

## New FSI Brief: ICE Was Holding None of 13,099 Noncitizens With Homicide Convictions

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026: The Founders' Square Institute today published Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy.

ICE reported to Congress that 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on the agency's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, inside a population of 425,431 convicted criminals ICE was not holding. Their records included 15,811 sexual assault convictions and 62,231 assault convictions. The non-detained docket now stands at 7.3 million aliens, against roughly 70,000 beds of ICE detention capacity.

The brief also documents at least 41,085 ICE detainers declined by sanctuary jurisdictions between October 2022 and early 2026, and 6,947 criminal illegal aliens released by New York during 2025 rather than transferred to ICE, including 29 with homicide offenses.

"These are the government's own numbers, not estimates and not advocacy," Kessler said. "ICE has identified more than 425,000 convicted criminals it is not holding, and it supervises a docket of 7.3 million people with about 70,000 beds. Congress funds those beds and writes the detention statutes, and neither has kept pace. Our recommendations are actionable this Congress: fund the beds, enforce detainer compliance, put 287(g) in statute, and make DHS report what it releases."

The brief recommends that Congress appropriate detention capacity above 90,000 beds; condition federal law enforcement grants on detainer compliance; codify and fund the 287(g) program, now at 2,246 active agreements; require quarterly publication of the criminal profile of the non-detained docket; and extend mandatory detention to aliens convicted of crimes of violence and sexual offenses.

The Founders' Square Institute is a nonpartisan public-policy think tank in Washington, D.C. Brief No. 14, its data appendix and a one-page fact sheet for Hill offices are available at fsi.org.
